tldr:
**Prompt caching** lets the API reuse the processing of a prompt's beginning (its **prefix**) when later requests start with exactly the same content. The order is tools, then system, then messages. This cuts processing time and cost for prompts that repeat a lot of fixed material: many examples, large background documents, the same long instructions every time, or long multi-turn conversations.

It **does not change the answer.** The docs say the response is identical to the one you'd get without caching. So it can make a working prompt faster and cheaper, but it can't fix a wrong one.

For the exam, you need to know it **exists** and what it's for. How to configure it is explicitly out of scope.
mentalModel: Prompt caching is a bookmark in a book you keep re-reading: it saves you re-reading the same opening pages, but only if they're word-for-word the same, and it never changes what the book says. The trap is picking it to fix a wrong, missed or stale answer. Caching makes a prompt faster, not better.
examNote: No task statement covers prompt caching. The guide's out-of-scope list puts its implementation details out of scope, apart from knowing that it exists (Guide §17 Appendix · Out-of-Scope Topics · p.39). So be ready to recognise it: know what problem it addresses (repeated identical prompt prefixes: latency and cost). Also know what it doesn't do, so you can reject it when an option offers it as the fix for a quality, context or correctness problem. You won't be asked to configure it.
whatItIs:
**Sub-concepts, each with a picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | What the docs say (paraphrased) | 🧭 Mental model |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What gets reused | The prefix of the prompt, in the order tools → system → messages, when it is **100% identical** to a previous request's. | A bookmark only helps if every page before it is the same, word for word. |
| 2 | What it's for | Repeated long material: many examples, large background context, the same instructions every time, long multi-turn conversations. It cuts processing time and cost. | Don't re-read the same opening chapters every time. |
| 3 | What it doesn't change | The output. The response is identical to the uncached one. | A faster photocopier, not a better writer: a wrong answer stays wrong. |
| 4 | It isn't memory | Each request still sends the full prompt. Caching reuses processing of an identical prefix; it doesn't give Claude, a subagent or a later session any new information. | The bookmark saves time; it doesn't remember what you learned. |
| 5 | Caching and batch together | Batches support prompt caching and the discounts can stack. Batch requests run asynchronously and concurrently, so cache hits inside a batch are best-effort. | Two separate levers: batch trades waiting time for cost, caching reuses an identical start. |

**Where you might meet it (my reading of the scenarios, not guide text):**

- **Customer support agent (Scenario 1):** every turn resends the same long system prompt and tool definitions. That's the kind of repeated prefix caching is for.
- **Structured data extraction (Scenario 6):** a large batch shares the same instructions and examples. Batch + caching can be combined.

In both, caching is an **efficiency** choice, never a fix for how well the agent behaves.

distractors.name: “Enable prompt caching” to stop the agent missing facts in the middle of long documents
distractors.looks: It's a long-context feature, so it sounds relevant.
distractors.fails: Caching doesn't change the output (docs): the same facts get missed, just faster.
distractors.instead: Fix the context: key facts summarised at the top, query at the end, trimmed tool output (D4.7).
distractors.source: 💡 my recommendation — from the docs: output is identical with or without caching

distractors.name: “Use prompt caching so the resumed session knows the code changed”
distractors.looks: Caching sounds like it keeps context “fresh”.
distractors.fails: It reuses an identical prefix; it adds no new information. Stale tool results stay stale.
distractors.instead: Tell the resumed session what changed, or start fresh with a summary (D1.4).
distractors.source: 💡 my recommendation — from the docs: caching reuses processing of an identical prefix

distractors.name: “Cache the coordinator's prompt so subagents inherit its context”
distractors.fails: A cache is not a channel between agents. A subagent only sees what's in its own prompt.
distractors.instead: Pass the needed context explicitly in the subagent's prompt (D1.2, D1.6).
distractors.source: 💡 my recommendation — from the docs: each request still sends its full prompt

distractors.name: “Use prompt caching instead of the Batch API for the overnight job”
distractors.looks: Both are described as ways to cut cost.
distractors.fails: They're different levers: batch trades latency for a discount (guide TS 4.5); caching reuses an identical prefix. They can be combined.
distractors.instead: Pick batch for work that can wait; add caching when many requests share the same long prefix.
distractors.source: 💡 my recommendation — from the batch docs: caching works with batches, discounts stack, hits best-effort

distractors.name: “Caching will make the extraction output consistent”
distractors.fails: Caching doesn't change what's generated; consistency comes from the prompt and the schema.
distractors.instead: Few-shot examples and a schema / structured output (D4.4, D4.9).

questions.q: An extraction pipeline sends 400-page contracts, and an audit finds it misses about 15% of clauses from the middle of each document. A teammate proposes enabling prompt caching, “since the model will have seen the document before”. What is the best response?
opts: Agree: caching lets the model re-read the cached document more carefully on each later request.
Agree, but cache only the middle section, where the missed clauses tend to appear most often.
Disagree: caching reuses processing of an identical prefix and doesn't change the output.
Disagree: caching works only for system prompts, so a document can't be cached in the first place.
questions.explain: Caching reuses the processing of an identical prompt prefix to save time and cost. The response is the same as without caching. Missed mid-document clauses are an attention problem, so restructure the context (D4.7) instead. A and B credit caching with an accuracy effect it doesn't have. D is false.

questions.q: A support agent must answer customers immediately. Every call resends the same 6,000-token system prompt and the same 14 tool definitions, and only the last few customer messages change. The team wants to cut the processing time and cost of the repeated part without delaying any reply. Which feature is designed for this?
questions.explain: Prompt caching reuses the processing of a repeated identical prefix (tools, then system, then messages) and doesn't delay responses. A is asynchronous, with no latency guarantee, so it doesn't fit a live chat. C changes the output limit. D shrinks history but does nothing for the repeated prefix.

questions.q: A manager reads that prompt caching “makes responses faster and cheaper” and asks whether turning it on will also change the extracted values on the team's 20,000 nightly invoices. Which statement is accurate?
opts: It returns the same response as without caching; it only reuses processing of an identical prefix.
It may return an earlier cached answer when two different invoices are similar enough to share a prefix.
It improves accuracy, because the cached prefix gets more attention on every later request.
It changes values only for batch requests, where cached and uncached processing can differ.
questions.explain: Caching doesn't change what the model outputs. It reuses the work of processing an identical prefix. B confuses prompt caching with response caching. C and D invent effects on output.

faq.q: Will the exam ask me how to configure prompt caching?
faq.a: Per the guide, no. Implementation details are out of scope beyond knowing that it exists (§17 Appendix · p.39). Know what it's for and what it doesn't fix.

faq.q: Why is it “D4.2” here if it's barely in the guide?
faq.a: The numbering comes from a community concept list (unverified) that this section mirrors for layout. The official guide decides scope, and it makes this topic awareness-only.

faq.q: Does caching make Claude remember earlier conversations?
faq.a: No. Each request still sends its full prompt. Caching only avoids re-processing a prefix identical to a recent request's.

faq.q: Does caching work with the Batch API?
faq.a: Yes, per the batch docs: the discounts can stack. Because batch requests run asynchronously and concurrently, cache hits there are best-effort.
